segments.source: Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.
Given facts.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should decide a dispute under law.
Rules.
Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar.
Task.
Should the request go first to the Local Court or the School Board? Why?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Identify the action: decide a dispute under law. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Local Court. 3. School Board has a different stated role, so it is not the first match.
Answer.
The request should go first to the Local Court.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.
Problem 613. Which institution has the role? Approve the town budget
Knowledge context.
Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.
Given facts.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should approve the town budget. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Rules.
Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Task.
Should the request go first to the Town Council or the Health Office? Why? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Identify the action: approve the town budget. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Town Council. 3. Health Office has a different stated role, so it is not the first match. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.
Answer.
The request should go first to the Town Council. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.
Problem 614. Which institution has the role? Organize the ballot count
Knowledge context.
Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.
Given facts.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should organize the ballot count. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 10 members, requires at least 6 present for quorum, and 8 are present.
Rules.

Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.
Task.
Should the request go first to the Election Committee or the Public Works Office? Why? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Identify the action: organize the ballot count. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Election Committee. 3. Public Works Office has a different stated role, so it is not the first match. Cross-domain check: compare 8 with 6; 8≥6 is true.
Answer.
The request should go first to the Election Committee. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.
